md: C and C++ do not check bounds or lifetimes for you. Every array index, every length and every `free` is a promise the programmer must keep by hand. Memory safety bugs are what happens when one promise is broken, and the attacker gets to choose the input.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Uninitialized memory and type confusion
md: Uninitialized reads leak what came before; type confusion reinterprets what is there. Both are fixed the same way in spirit: never let code read bytes whose meaning it has not established, by initializing first and checking tags before use.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: ArcFace: putting an angular margin inside a classifier
md: The class weights only cover training identities. At test time you discard them and compare normalized features with cosine similarity, exactly as with a triplet-trained model. A large classification accuracy on training classes is not the goal.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
md: Noise you can see and average away; bias you cannot. Vary the setup (layout, link order, process, machine) and trust only effects that survive the variation.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Bitwise-equal logprobs do not make an async run on-policy. True-on-policy alignment removes numerical mismatch between engines, not staleness from training on groups generated under older weights; the data buffer bounds that separately.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The attacker holds the phone: OWASP MAS and its threat model
md: Treat everything inside the app as readable and changeable by its user. The app's job is to protect the user's data from *other* parties (other apps, thieves, the network). Decisions about what a user is allowed to do belong on the server.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: WebViews: a browser inside the app, with a bridge to native code
md: A WebView bridge turns 'which page is loaded' into 'who can call our native code'. Control both: what may load, and which origin each bridge call came from.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Absorbing the up-projections: attend in latent space
md: Absorption is just regrouping a product of matrices: $q^{\top}(W c) = (W^{\top} q)^{\top} c$. It turns MLA decoding into MQA-shaped work over the latent cache, so no per-head key or value is ever stored or rebuilt.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Merge when one adapter dominates the traffic and per-token latency matters most. Keep adapters unmerged when many adapters are active concurrently, so the base matmul can be batched across all of them.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Asking for diversity cuts both ways. Raudaschl's repo has a diverse mode whose prompt asks for synonyms, broader or narrower framings and related sub-topics, and to avoid minor rewordings. That reduces redundancy but pushes phrasings toward the edge of the topic, where drift lives. Inspect generated queries on real traffic before tuning N.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Multi-token prediction keeps the input and the causal context the same and only adds targets: each position is asked for tokens t+1 through t+n, all from the prefix ending at t.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why orthogonalize: steepest descent under the spectral norm
md: This argument explains the *direction* of a single step, with moving averages switched off. It says nothing about momentum: Bernstein and Newhouse treat the averages as smoothing against mini-batch noise, and call their exact role an open question. Muon adds momentum for empirical reasons.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
md: An optimizer claim is only as good as its baseline. Ask: was the baseline tuned as hard, at more than one scale and data ratio, compared at the end of training, and in which unit (steps, tokens, FLOPs or hours)? Independent tests put matrix optimizers ahead of AdamW, by less than first reported.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Deriving the rules from one condition, and muP by hand
md: One rule generates muP: every weight and every update should have spectral norm about the square root of fan_out over fan_in. For Adam that means learning rate 1/fan_in for every layer; for SGD, fan_out/fan_in.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: Atomic does not mean cheap. An atomic write to a line that other cores are reading forces cache-line transfers, and in Bos's measurement it made another core's plain loads about 10 times slower on an older x86-64 machine.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC trades space for concurrency: every update leaves an old version behind so that readers already in flight can keep a consistent view without blocking writers.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
md: MVCC moves the cost of concurrency into the storage engine: dead versions to clean, index entries to maintain, and XIDs to freeze. Long-lived snapshots make all three worse.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
md: The gates are independent sigmoids, not a softmax. They do not have to sum to 1, so the model can turn several branches up or down at once. Also note what NSA does *not* do: it keeps the full KV cache (and three branches with independent keys and values), so it cuts the bytes *read* per step, not the bytes *stored*.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
md: MIH is fast only when substring buckets stay small. Norouzi et al. analyze uniformly distributed codes and find a substring length of about log2 of the database size works well. Highly skewed hashes (many near-blank images with the same hash) create giant buckets. PDQ's quality score, a 0 to 100 measure of how much detail an image has (next lesson), flags such featureless images so they can be filtered out.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Running for real: metrics, checkpoints, export and a multi-node recipe
md: In all three published runs generation takes about half the step or more. Read your own `timing/train/` split before tuning: if generation dominates, the levers are vLLM parallelism and memory (lesson 4), non-colocated async generation (lesson 5) and response length, not the training backend.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: RST injection and the history of TCP session hijacking
md: Address-based trust is the real bug behind classic hijacking. Any system that grants access because a packet claims a source IP (old rsh, IP allow lists alone, zone transfers allowed by address) is relying on something an attacker can forge. Use cryptographic authentication.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: From overview to stream: the Wireshark workflow, decryption and tshark
md: A key log file is the key to every session it lists. Treat it like a password file: create it only for test traffic on your own machine, store it with the capture under the same protection, and delete both when done. Never set SSLKEYLOGFILE on a machine others use.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Extracting files from traffic: reassembly, true types and hashes
md: A hash lookup that returns nothing does not mean a file is safe: new and targeted malware is unknown by definition. Treat unknown executables from unusual sources as suspicious until analysed.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Routing: gateways, TTL, traceroute and BGP
md: Routing is decided hop by hop from tables, and the most specific matching prefix wins. On the internet those tables are built from announcements other networks make, which BGP accepts on trust unless someone filters or validates them.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
md: Reading is not touching. The `mbind(2)` man page notes that a first *read* of an anonymous page maps a shared page of zeros held by the kernel; no page is allocated on your node until the first *write*. A warm-up loop that only reads does not place anything.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Garbage collection and the write amplification formula
md: A drive does not know which LBAs your file system considers free. Unless told (lesson 4), every LBA ever written counts as live. Agrawal et al. put it bluntly: unlike a log-structured file system (one that, like an FTL, appends every write to a log and cleans it, but knows which files were deleted), the disk here is always full, so cleaning pressure is maximal all the time.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
md: AP measures ranking quality across all thresholds for one class; COCO mAP averages it over 10 IoU thresholds and all classes. When comparing papers, check which one is reported: AP50 and AP@[.5:.95] differ a lot for the same model.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Tiered storage versus S3-native: choosing a design
md: Tiered storage moves *old* data to S3 and leaves the write path alone. S3-native moves the *write path itself* to S3, trading commit latency for stateless compute. Hybrids like Neon put a small quorum log in front so commits stay fast while object storage holds the bulk.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
md: Alert on symptoms, not causes. The SRE book's advice is to focus much more effort on catching symptoms than causes, and to worry about a cause only when it is very definite and very imminent. A page saying "cache hit rate dropped" is a cause; a page saying "users are burning the checkout budget at 20x" is a symptom, and it stays correct when the cause next time is something else.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Adding layout: from LayoutLM boxes to OCR-free Donut
md: Layout-aware models add *where* to *what*: each word's box becomes embedding lookups, so a model can learn that a value sits right of its key. OCR-free models fold reading into the network and emit structure directly.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Linux capabilities: splitting root into pieces
md: `docker run --privileged` gives the container all capabilities and access to all host devices (Docker documentation). Treat it as running the workload as root on the host. The same goes for adding `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` or `CAP_SYS_MODULE` "just for one feature".

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Ethics and law first: public is not the same as permitted
md: Red lines in this course: no locating, profiling or tracking of specific private individuals; no misrepresentation to get access; no use of credentials or data from breaches; no publishing of personal details. Worked examples use your own organisation, a fictional company (Northwind, under the reserved `.example` domain) or public institutions and already-public cases.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Metadata: what photos and documents say about themselves
md: Files describe themselves. Read metadata as one clue that needs corroboration; remove it from everything you publish.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: People-search sites, data brokers and protecting your own footprint
md: Check only your own accounts, or colleagues' with their consent. Looking up someone else's email in breach data or a broker profile, without a lawful basis, is exactly the profiling this course rules out.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
md: Declare every real dependency on the target that uses it, with the narrowest correct scope: PRIVATE if only the .cpp files use it, PUBLIC if your headers expose it, INTERFACE if only your headers do. CMake then derives include paths, definitions and link order for you.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Do not add `@pytest.mark.flaky` or `xfail` to a test your PR broke. Maintainers read that as hiding a failure. If you believe a failure is pre-existing flakiness, show evidence: the same test failing on `main` or on other PRs, or a seed that reproduces it without your change.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: You may not add a Reviewed-by, Tested-by or Acked-by tag for someone just because they said nice things. The kernel guide says these need the named person's explicit permission; only Cc:, Reported-by: and Suggested-by: can be added with implicit permission.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
md: Before using an AI tool on a contribution, find the project's policy (CONTRIBUTING, developer docs, or the docs on patch submission). Then: never submit what you cannot explain, disclose as the project asks, and never let a tool add your sign-off.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
md: `--force-with-lease` says "overwrite only if the remote is still what I last fetched". Add `--force-if-includes` so a fetch alone does not count as having seen the remote's commits.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: The most common CLA failure is an email mismatch: the commits use a personal or unregistered address while the agreement (or the employer's group) lists another. Fix the author email and rewrite the commits, not the agreement.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? t-tests, U tests and p-values
md: Significant is not the same as large. benchstat's docs stress that with enough low-noise data even very small changes become significant. Report the size of the change and its spread, and use the test only to answer "is this more than noise?"

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A bug report's first job is to let the maintainer make the failure happen themselves. Everything else in the report (description, guesses about the cause) comes second.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
md: A flaky repro is not done until it fails every time or you know its failure rate. Pin seeds and inputs, report versions, and repeat runs enough times that a PASS means something.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
md: Self-review first, then mark ready. A reviewable PR is focused, explained, clean, and honestly labeled as draft or ready.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
md: Prefix caching never changes outputs. It reuses KV for exactly the same tokens instead of recomputing it, so its effects are on speed and memory (outputs can differ only by the tiny floating-point noise any change in batching causes). It helps exactly as much as prefill dominates the work and prefixes repeat.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Verifying findings safely, without becoming the incident
md: Verify with the least risky evidence that answers the question. Write down the confidence and what you chose not to do. Stop immediately when you see signs that someone else got there first.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Broken stacks: frame pointers, DWARF, LBR and symbols
md: Missing callers, a detached tower over [unknown], or hex instead of names are not hot spots. They are profiler blind spots. Fix frame pointers or symbols before you trust the picture.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Why people are the most attacked surface
md: The one thing to remember: phishing attacks a decision, not a machine. Defences therefore come in three kinds: stop the message arriving, make the action harmless if taken (for example passkeys, logins that only work on the real site; lesson 12), and make the final step need a second check (for example calling the supplier on a known number).

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Lookalike domains and homoglyphs
md: Misconception: "hover over the link and check the domain" solves this. A homoglyph domain can look correct even when you hover, and on phones you often cannot hover. Machine checks (skeletons, domain age) and phishing-resistant logins (lesson 12) carry the load; human checks are a backup.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Byte order: reading and writing multi-byte fields on the wire
md: Wire formats fix two things: where each field sits and the byte order inside it. Pick the order in the format's specification, then convert at the edge with shifts, `from_be_bytes` or `ntohl`, and keep ordinary structs inside the program.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Real-time tracking, 3D lifting and joint angles for apps
md: Keypoints are noisy, especially when occluded. Before writing rules on them: check per-keypoint visibility or score, prefer 3D world landmarks or a side view for sagittal angles (bends in the side-view plane that splits the body into left and right) such as the knee, smooth over a few frames, and use two thresholds (hysteresis) rather than one.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Crypto inventory and agility: finding every RSA before 2030
md: Agility has a price you met in tls-pki: anything that negotiates can be **downgraded**. Keep the allowed list short, remove algorithms rather than leaving them enabled "just in case", and authenticate the negotiation (as TLS 1.3 does by signing the transcript). An unauthenticated algorithm field is an attacker's choice, not yours.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: **The one thing to remember:** ask whether the next address is known before the current load finishes. If not, you are latency-bound and more bandwidth will not help. If yes, you are probably bandwidth-bound and the question becomes how many bytes you move.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Pseudonyms and hashes are not anonymity: AOL 2006
md: A hash of an identifier is an identifier. Anyone who can guess the input space (all phone numbers, all emails in a leaked list) can reverse it. Use a keyed HMAC for pseudonyms, and remember that pseudonymised data is still personal data.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy: a promise about one person
md: DP does not promise that nothing can be learned about you. If a study shows smoking causes cancer, a smoker's insurer learns something. DP promises that the result would have been about the same whether or not *your* data was in it.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Designing for less: data minimisation and purpose limitation
md: "We might need it later" is not a purpose. Data collected without a specified purpose fails GDPR Article 5(1)(b) and becomes an unreviewed liability in every copy.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Rights in code: access and erasure across every copy
md: Deleting the primary row is not erasure. Without a data map, copies in analytics, tickets, partners and backups survive, and the reply you sent the user is false.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket: why a hash works like a password
md: A hash or ticket is a password-equivalent. Protect where it is cached, make each one valid in as few places as possible, and watch for valid logons in the wrong context: right account, wrong machine, wrong protocol, wrong time.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: What should a step reward measure? Value, progress, implicit PRMs
md: Value says how promising a prefix is; progress (an advantage) says whether this step helped. Progress is the better step reward, if measured under a complementary prover. Implicit PRMs get Q values for free from an outcome model trained as a log ratio, and PRIME keeps that model fresh with online updates.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a context switch, step by step
md: Register save and restore is the same for every switch. The difference between a thread switch and a process switch is the address space: if `next` shares `prev`'s memory, the page table stays loaded and the TLB stays valid.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Distances from codes: lookup tables, SDC and ADC
md: ADC = exact query, quantized database. Per query you build an $m \times k^*$ table once, then each database vector costs $m$ lookups and adds. This is why PQ scans are fast and why everyone uses ADC.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Sequence recovery is a proxy, not a goal. A design that recovers 100 percent of a natural sequence has designed nothing new, and a design that recovers 30 percent may fold perfectly well. Recovery is useful only because it correlates with getting the physics right. What you actually test is whether the designed sequence folds back to the backbone you asked for.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Files, functions and exceptions: scripts that survive bad input
md: Read files with `with open(..., encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")`, put reusable steps in functions, and catch only the exceptions you can handle. A missing log is a finding, not a zero.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Safe coding habits: no eval, no shell strings, no secrets in code
md: Data is never code. Parse it with a format-specific parser, pass it to other programs as list arguments, validate it against what it should be, and keep secrets in the environment, not in the file.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Conversational rewriting: turning a follow-up into a standalone query
md: Misconception: the rewriter should make the query richer. Its job is to make it *standalone and faithful*. A rewriter that adds guessed facts (say, "when the leader fails during a network partition") can steer retrieval toward documents the user never asked about. Instruct it not to answer, and to return the message unchanged when it is already standalone.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound
md: Per vector, the query-time work is a few AND plus popcount passes over the D-bit code and a handful of multiply-adds with precomputed factors. The error bound then tells you which candidates are worth an exact distance.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Race conditions from zero: concurrency, the race window and TOCTOU
md: A lock inside one process (threading.Lock here) protects only threads in that process. A web app with several worker processes or servers needs the lock where the state lives, usually in the database (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Why "too fast to exploit" fails: jitter and the single-packet attack
md: The single-packet attack made network distance irrelevant: a tester far away can now hit a 1 ms window about as reliably as one on the same network. Treat every check-then-act as reachable, and fix it with atomicity, not with speed.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft log replication: AppendEntries, nextIndex and commit
md: Stored on a majority is not the same as committed. An entry from an *earlier* term can sit on a majority and still be erased by a later leader. Commitment is only decided by counting replicas of an entry from the leader's *current* term, which then commits everything before it.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: What a ranker sees: one feature vector per query-document pair
md: A ranking model only knows what its feature vector tells it. If a signal that decides relevance (freshness for news, location for local search) is not encoded as a number for each query-document pair, no amount of model tuning can recover it.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: ERR: a user who stops once satisfied
md: **$g_{\max}$ is a convention, and tools hard-code it.** TREC's `gdeval.pl` (the official Web track script, which ir_measures used for `ERR@5` in our test) sets `MAX_JUDGMENT = 4`. With our 0 to 3 grades, gdeval gives Run A an ERR@5 of 0.240, not 0.452, and Run B 0.438, not 0.875. Rankings of runs may survive, but the numbers cannot be compared with an ERR computed under $g_{\max} = 3$.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Change Healthcare and ALPHV, February 2024
md: One remote access portal without MFA, at one subsidiary, gave a criminal nine quiet days. Inventory every remote access path (VPNs, Citrix, RDP gateways, vendor portals, acquired companies' systems) and enforce MFA on all of them, then test that it is enforced.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
md: An (address, rkey) pair is a capability: whoever holds it, on a QP in the same protection domain, can read or write that memory with no further check by your CPU. Grant the narrowest access flags you need, and revoke by deregistering (`ibv_dereg_mr`) or with memory windows, which the manual describes as a cheaper way to grant and revoke remote access dynamically.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Client-side prediction and server reconciliation
md: Each server state is a statement about the past: "here is the world after your input #n". Reset to it, then replay inputs after #n. Sequence numbers are what make that subtraction possible.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Two-stage systems: candidate generation, two towers, ranking
md: Retrieval must be cheap per item (dot products over precomputed vectors); ranking can be expensive per item. In-batch negatives are sampled by popularity, so correct each logit by log p_j.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: A query plan is a tree of operators that pull rows
md: Cost units are not milliseconds. They are relative estimates the planner uses to compare plans. To see real time, use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which actually runs the query.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leader replication: when is a commit really safe?
md: A commit is only as safe as the set of machines that had it when the client was told "ok". Every replication knob is a choice of *how many* and *which* machines that set must include, paid for in commit latency.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: What RLHF reward hacking looks like: length, sycophancy, persuasion
md: Misconception: longer answers after RLHF just mean a more helpful model. Sometimes length carries real information. But when the reward gain mostly vanishes once you compare answers of equal length, the policy has optimized a correlate of quality, not quality. Report output length next to every reward and win rate.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
md: A common misconception: "security owns security risk". In every framework in this course, the **business owner** of a system owns its risk and the decision to accept it. The security team advises, measures and challenges. When security silently accepts risk on the business's behalf, nobody with budget or authority knows the risk exists.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Treating risk: accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid
md: Every risk ends in one of four decisions, recorded with an owner and a date. Compare options in money: expected yearly loss plus treatment cost for the average, and tail percentiles for survival. Mitigation usually wins on average; insurance wins on the tail; avoidance can win on both.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: PCI DSS v4: the cardholder data environment and scoping
md: PCI DSS is a contractual standard with 12 requirements. Scope is the CDE plus anything connected to it or able to affect it, so reduce scope first: segment, and better, never touch card numbers (tokenise with a payment provider). What remains on your side, especially the payment page's scripts, must be inventoried and watched.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Policies people follow and awareness that works
md: Policies: short, owned, true, enforced by guardrails, with an exception path and a review date. Awareness: required by every framework, but measure it honestly; put the weight on controls that make human mistakes survivable, and on making reporting easy.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
md: Partial rollouts are not free. A trajectory stitched from segments generated by several policy versions is off-policy data. Kimi notes some segments can be excluded from the loss; AReaL's interruptible rollouts face the same issue and handle it with a modified PPO objective.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Multi-turn agentic rollouts: tools, servers and token-in, token-out
md: Agentic rollouts move the bottleneck from decode length to tool latency. Run each trajectory as its own coroutine against continuous-batching servers, route a conversation's turns to the same server, scale tools as separate services, and pass exact token ids and logprobs to the trainer.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: MTTR: detect, triage, mitigate, resolve
md: Mitigating destroys evidence. Reverting the config drains the queue, restarts pods and rotates the logs that held the smoking gun. Before you revert, spend the 30 seconds: snapshot the pool metrics, grab one stack dump, copy the rendered config, note the exact timestamps. The chapter's phrase is that rapid triage does not preclude preserving evidence of what is going wrong.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Weighted RRF and multi-query fusion (RAG-Fusion)
md: Multi-query fusion has costs. In the Infineon study RAG-Fusion averaged 34.62 s versus 19.52 s for plain RAG (1.77 times slower in that deployment), mostly from the larger answer call, and some answers strayed off topic when the generated queries were not relevant enough. If the rewrites are near-duplicates, fusion just re-counts the same list.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Objects the C side owns: ARef, AlwaysRefCounted and RCU
md: Two ways to use an object you did not allocate: hold an `ARef<T>` when you need it to stay alive *across time* (stored in a struct, sent to another thread), or borrow it under an `rcu::Guard` when you only need it *briefly* and the data is RCU-protected. The first costs a refcount increment; the second costs almost nothing but forbids sleeping until the guard is dropped.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
md: Inserting a task into a local DSQ is a commitment. Once there, it waits for that CPU even if another CPU goes idle a microsecond later. Schedulers that want work sharing keep tasks in a shared custom DSQ and move them to a local DSQ only when a CPU asks via `ops.dispatch()`.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality
md: Misconception: if no idle CPU was found, a busy CPU will pick the task up soon. Only CPUs that run their dispatch path do, and idle tracking races with CPUs going idle. Inserting into a queue no CPU will look at, with no kick, is how schedulers stall while CPUs idle.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Hard-coded credentials (CWE-798) and why deleting them fails
md: Environment variables are a stepping stone, not the goal. OWASP's Secrets Management Cheat Sheet warns that environment variables "are generally accessible to all processes and may be included in logs or system dumps". Prefer files or APIs that the platform injects at runtime, readable only by the one process that needs them.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: What a secure code reviewer is looking for
md: A misconception: "the tests pass, so it is safe". Tests show the code does what was intended for the inputs someone thought of. A security review asks about inputs nobody thought of. Every bug in this course passed its author's tests.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Regular expressions that hang: ReDoS and the Cloudflare outage
md: Patterns written to *detect* attacks are code too. Cloudflare's outage came from a security rule, deployed globally within seconds because security rules must ship fast. Review regexes in WAF rules, input validators and log parsers with the same care as application code, and test them against long near-miss strings, not only against strings that match.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: what safe Rust promises, and reviewing unsafe
md: Review unsafe Rust as C, with one question: can any input from safe code make this block break its preconditions? Require a SAFETY comment that names the check, keep the block tiny, think about panics in the middle, and run the tests under Miri.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IKEv2: four messages to build the keys and the first tunnel
md: IKE_SA_INIT agrees on keys but proves nothing about who is on the other end; a man-in-the-middle could complete it. Authentication happens only in IKE_AUTH, where AUTH binds each peer's credential to the earlier messages. If AUTH is weak (a guessable pre-shared key), the whole tunnel is weak, however strong the Diffie-Hellman group.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: What security architecture is: where every control sits
md: Architecture is placement. For each trust boundary, name the enforcement point, check that nothing can go around it, and list what it depends on. Those dependencies are your trusted computing base, and they deserve the most scrutiny.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: NIST SP 800-207: the logical architecture of zero trust
md: Zero trust concentrates trust in the policy engine, the administrator, the identity provider and the device inventory. Protect them as the most critical systems you run, and treat a change to access policy as a security event.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Queues: acknowledge fast, process later, expect duplicates
md: A longer visibility timeout reduces duplicates from slow workers. It never removes duplicates from storage redundancy or redelivery. The handler must be safe to run twice, whatever the queue settings.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: AI for finding bugs, reviewing code and writing detections
md: A rule that never fires looks exactly like a quiet network. Every detection, human or AI written, ships with samples it must match and samples it must not.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: How a vulnerability becomes public: disclosure, CVE and NVD
md: "Zero-day" describes the defenders' situation (no fix existed), not how clever the attack is. Most real breaches use **known** vulnerabilities with patches available for weeks or years. Equifax (lesson 8) is the textbook example.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Defence in depth: layers, and why they must be independent
md: Defence in depth means several *different* layers across Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, so that one failure does not mean total failure. The math only works when layers fail independently: hunt down shared passwords, shared admin accounts and silent monitoring first.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Maturity models: measuring where you are with C2M2 levels
md: A maturity score measures capability, not outcomes. A domain at MIL3 can still miss an intrusion, and self-evaluations drift upward when the people scoring are the people judged. Ask for evidence for each "Fully Implemented", and pair the maturity view with outcome metrics (lesson 8).

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Designing the team: functions, coverage and where people sit
md: Single points of failure apply to people. If one engineer is the only person who understands the detection pipeline or the privileged access management (PAM) vault that holds admin passwords, the programme fails when they go on leave or resign. Recall from the appsec course how Equifax's patch alert went to a mailing list for roles that had no named owner. Pair people, document runbooks, rotate duties.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Writing is a security control: Equifax's patch email
md: A security message is a control with a single point of failure: the reader. Write it to one accountable person, say what to do and by when, and say what happens if they do not answer.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Writing for disclosure: vendor reports, advisories and Project Zero
md: Disclosure writing is for action: give the vendor everything needed to reproduce and fix, give the public what they need to know if they are affected and what to do, and state your timeline at the start.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Playing against your past self: SPIN and Self-Rewarding LMs
md: SPIN's fixed point is the human data distribution. It can extract more from an SFT dataset than plain SFT does, but it cannot surpass that data: once the model's responses are indistinguishable from the human ones, the loss gives no signal.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Provider prompt caching is a different thing from semantic caching
md: They stack. Check the semantic cache first; on a miss, send a request whose stable content comes first so the provider's prefix cache can reuse it. Prompt caching is safe to turn on everywhere; a semantic cache needs the threshold and scoping work from the previous lessons.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell: how logging a string ran code
md: Log4Shell is injection in a place nobody thought was an interpreter. Logging user input is normal and correct; the library silently treated part of that input as template syntax with network access. Recall the injection course: whenever data is evaluated, the evaluator is the attack surface.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
md: Chunked prefill trades the long prompt's time to first token for bounded step size: lower peak activation memory (activations are the intermediate tensors a forward pass keeps, and they grow with the number of tokens in the pass) and, when decodes are mixed in, steadier token gaps for everyone else. It does not reduce total prefill work.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: CH trades a one-time preprocessing pass (contract nodes, add shortcuts) for tiny queries: two upward searches that meet at the most important node of the route, then shortcuts are unpacked back into original roads.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: Misconception: "wider vectors always mean proportionally faster code." Width is only the upper bound. Memory bandwidth, latency chains and loop overheads decide how much of it you actually get.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
md: Allocators are not just faster or slower `malloc`s. Each design gives up a freedom (free in any order, any size, any type) and gets speed or lower fragmentation in return. Ask which freedom your workload can give up.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: "Disaggregated" here is about trainer versus rollout GPUs. It is unrelated to PD (prefill-decode) disaggregation (`--prefill-num-servers`), which puts SGLang's prefill (processing the whole prompt in one pass) and decode (generating one token at a time) on different servers, and it does not imply async training by itself.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Verdicts, severity and priority: true, false and benign positives
md: Using a rule's historical precision in priority has a trap: a rule that is usually wrong will sink to the bottom forever, including the one time it is right. Precision should make you fix the rule, not ignore it. Target's "malware.binary" alerts are the cautionary tale.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Pivoting, building a timeline, and mapping it to ATT&CK
md: Do not force-fit. If you cannot say which technique an event shows, write the plain fact and leave the ID out. A wrong mapping in a case note propagates into reports and detection gap analyses.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Voice clones and deepfake meetings: when seeing is not believing
md: Misconception: "train people to spot deepfakes". Spotting artefacts is a losing race as tools improve, and the IC3 itself says AI content is often hard to identify. Teach the artefacts as a reason to pause, but make the decision depend on an independent channel.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Why single neurons are hard to read: superposition
md: Superposition: a layer with $d$ dimensions can represent many more than $d$ sparse features as almost-orthogonal directions, at the cost of interference. Neurons then mix many features, so we look for directions instead.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Reading a latent: activating examples, logit effects, autointerp
md: A Neuronpedia label is an LLM's guess from a sample of examples, not ground truth. Before you build on a latent, read examples from its lower activation intervals and a few non-activating contexts that seem to match the name.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Inverse distance weighting: weights from distance alone
md: IDW ignores how sensors sit relative to each other. S1 and S2 are only 2.24 km apart and both read 11, so they carry nearly the same information. IDW still counts both at full weight. If ten sensors sat in one parking lot, IDW would let that lot outvote everything else. Kriging, later in the course, fixes this.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Why decoding is slow and why checking guesses is cheap
md: Decoding is slow because each step moves all the weights to produce one token. Checking $K$ guessed tokens in one target pass moves the weights once, so every accepted guess is a target step you did not pay for.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
md: Mel settings are not interchangeable. librosa defaults to the Slaney scale, while `torchaudio.transforms.MelSpectrogram` defaults to `mel_scale='htk'` and `n_mels=128`. Features computed with different settings than a model was trained on look like a different microphone to the model.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
md: The stack is not faster *memory*. Stack and heap bytes live in the same RAM behind the same caches. What is cheaper is *allocation*: one `sub` on `rsp` versus a search through allocator data structures. The top of the stack is also almost always hot in cache because it is reused constantly.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
md: Huge pages are not free. The THP documentation warns that a process that maps a large region but touches one byte can get a whole 2 MiB page instead of 4 KiB, and allocating a huge page needs 2 MiB of *physically contiguous* memory, which may require compaction: the kernel moves in-use pages around to assemble a free contiguous run. That is why `madvise` mode exists.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
md: LLM judges are convenient but not neutral. CAA used GPT-4 to score open-ended answers from 1 to 10 and notes the scores are sensitive to the rubric's wording; they spot-checked against their own ratings. String-matching refusal detectors have the opposite problem: they catch "I'm sorry" but not a harmful reply, so Arditi et al. paired them with Llama Guard 2.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
md: Two different knobs, often confused. The bound $B$ moves the watermark (how long to wait before the first result). The allowed lateness $L$ keeps state after that (how long to accept corrections). Raising $B$ delays every result; raising $L$ costs state memory and extra firings but does not delay the first result.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens
md: Attention output for a position = softmax(its query dotted with every key, divided by the square root of d_k), used as weights on the value vectors. Every step is a matrix multiply or a row-wise softmax, so all positions are computed at once.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
md: One layer: attention adds a cross-position change, add & norm, the FFN adds a per-position change, add & norm. At inference the encoder runs once and the decoder runs once per output token, with beam search choosing among the most probable partial outputs.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25 in Lucene and Elasticsearch: fields, tuning, limits
md: BM25 only matches the terms you typed, after analysis. A document saying "low-cost airfare" scores 0 for cheap flights. Synonyms, stemming, query expansion (adding related terms to the query), or a dense retriever (a neural network maps query and documents to vectors, ranked by vector similarity) are needed for vocabulary mismatch, which is why many systems combine BM25 with vector search.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
md: The training loop is the generic one (forward, cross-entropy, backward, clip, AdamW step), and the GPT-specific knowledge is in the settings: small normal init with scaled residual projections, decoupled weight decay on matrices only, warmup then cosine decay, and big token batches via gradient accumulation.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Integrals: accumulated change and area under a curve
md: An integral adds up infinitely many thin slices $f(x)\,dx$. To evaluate one, find an antiderivative and subtract its values at the ends; when no antiderivative is available, add up trapezoids numerically.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Jacobians: derivatives of vector-valued functions
md: The Jacobian generalizes the derivative to vector outputs, and the chain rule becomes a product of Jacobians. Backprop never forms those matrices: it carries one row (the loss gradient) backward and multiplies it into each layer's Jacobian, giving $W^\top$ products for inputs and outer products for weights.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions
md: `if`, `while`, `&&` and `||` all branch on an exit status. `[` and `test` are commands that turn a comparison into a status. Functions return a status with `return` and data on standard output.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Job control and signals: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, background jobs and trap
md: Reaching for `kill -9` first is a habit worth breaking. SIGKILL gives the program no chance to flush buffered output, remove lock or temporary files, or stop its own child processes, which can be left running as orphans. Send SIGTERM, give it a few seconds, then escalate.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
md: Static word embeddings (one fixed vector per word, whatever the sentence) encode co-occurrence statistics. Similar vectors mean *used in similar contexts*, which often but not always means *similar meaning*: antonyms like hot and cold share many contexts too.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
md: Prefill is math-bound (many tokens share each weight read). Decode is memory-bound (one token per weight read). Most GPU time in a long answer goes to decode, and the floor for each decode step is weight bytes divided by bandwidth.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes and hex: how numbers are stored
md: Bits have no type. The byte `0xf4` is 244, or -12, or part of a jump instruction, depending on which instruction reads it. Hex is a compact way to write bits: one digit for every 4 bits.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
md: Simplified model. Real CPUs have several cache levels, and **hardware prefetchers** detect sequential and strided access (every k-th element, a fixed step apart) and fetch lines before they are asked for, hiding much of the cost of row order (and some of column order). Measured slowdowns vary by machine; the direction does not.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From web crawl to training tokens: the pretraining data pipeline
md: More deduplication is not automatically better. FineWeb first deduplicated all 96 snapshots against each other, which left 4T tokens and barely beat no deduplication. In the oldest snapshot, the 10 percent of data that survived was worse than the 90 percent removed (more ads and keyword lists). Deduplicating each snapshot on its own, about 20T tokens, matched the strong RefinedWeb dataset.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Policy gradients: how a score becomes a gradient
md: Policy gradient = average of advantage times the gradient of the log-probability of what was sampled. Baselines and value models cut the noise without biasing it, GAE spreads one final score into per-token advantages, and the ratio rho lets one batch of samples be reused.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
md: The base of the log in idf does not change the ranking: switching from log10 to ln multiplies every idf by the same constant (about 2.303), so every score scales equally. What does matter is the shape, for example whether tf is raw or sublinear.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Multi-file C: headers, include guards, static, extern and make
md: A missing header in a prerequisite list gives silent stale builds. With `main.o: main.c` only, changing SQUARE to a cube in square.h rebuilt area.o alone, and app still printed 9 instead of 27. List every header, or let the compiler do it: `-MMD` makes GCC and Clang write a .d file of each source's user-header dependencies for the Makefile to include.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
md: Every malloc needs exactly one matching free, on every path out of the function. Missing it leaks memory; doing it twice, or touching the block afterwards, is undefined behavior that can corrupt the allocator's own bookkeeping.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
md: 'It runs fine' is not evidence that C code is correct. A clean run without sanitizers says almost nothing about memory safety; even a clean sanitizer run covers only the paths your inputs exercised.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
md: Assigning, passing, or returning a non-`Copy` value moves it. To keep using the original, either `clone()` it (pay for a copy) or lend it out with a reference (next lesson).

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
md: `clone()` everywhere and `Rc<RefCell<T>>` everywhere make errors go away but give up what ownership buys you: clones cost time and memory, and `RefCell` turns compile-time guarantees into run-time panics. Reach for them when the data really has no single owner, not to silence the checker.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
md: Not every useful function is linear. $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} \ne 0$ is **affine**: it moves the origin, so $f(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{b}$ instead of $\mathbf{0}$. Neural network layers are affine, and their activation functions (like ReLU, explained next) are not linear at all. That nonlinearity is what lets a deep network do more than one big matrix could.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The SVD: rotate, stretch, rotate, then keep what matters
md: Every matrix is rotate, stretch, rotate: $A = U\Sigma V^\top$. $\sigma_1$ is the spectral norm, $\sigma_1/\sigma_n$ the condition number, the count of nonzero $\sigma_i$ the rank. Truncating to the top $r$ terms is the best rank-$r$ approximation, and PCA is the SVD of centered data.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Many features: linear regression in matrix form and feature scaling
md: Compute $\mu$ and $\sigma$ on the **training** data only and reuse those same numbers for validation, test and production inputs. Computing them on all the data leaks information from the held-out rows into training (lesson 11).

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Bias and variance: where the U-shaped test curve comes from
md: High variance is not the same as high training error. The degree-9 fit has zero training error and the largest variance; its errors show up only on new data.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
md: A hidden layer only adds power because of the nonlinearity between layers. Without it, any stack of layers is one linear map in disguise.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The cost of backprop: compute, activation memory, checkpointing
md: Backprop's compute is a small constant times the forward pass, about two more matrix multiplies per layer. Its memory is the real constraint: every activation from the forward pass stays alive until its layer's backward step, unless you pay compute to recompute it.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB
md: The offset is never translated, and the page table is per process. Two processes can use the same virtual address 21 and reach completely different physical bytes; that is the isolation, not a bug.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock
md: A deadlock-prone program can run correctly many times, because the deadlock needs an unlucky interleaving. Testing does not show it is safe; a lock order does.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
md: Independent is not the same as mutually exclusive. Mutually exclusive events ("sum is 2" and "sum is 12") cannot both happen, so learning one happened tells you the other did not: they are strongly *dependent*. Independence means the joint probability factorizes, $P(A \cap C) = P(A)P(C)$.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Why averages are stable: the law of large numbers and the CLT
md: Noise in an average shrinks as $1/\sqrt n$. That single scaling law explains why larger batches give smoother gradients, why small evals are noisy, and why A/B tests need large samples to detect small effects.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
md: Every test in this lesson is the same move: estimate, compute its standard error from the variance rules and the CLT, and ask how many standard errors the estimate sits from the null. Significance depends on sample size as much as on effect size.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars
md: Never report a scaling-law forecast without two checks: refit from several starts with tight tolerances and confirm they agree, and bootstrap the runs to get a range. A single unconverged fit can be off by 2x and still look perfectly reasonable.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first
md: IDCG must come from **all** judged documents in the qrels, not from re-sorting the documents your run retrieved. Re-sorting only the retrieved ones gives IDCG 5.193 and nDCG@10 = 0.674 instead of 0.576, and hides the fact that the run missed d9 entirely. trec_eval builds the ideal from the qrels.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Training embeddings with in-batch negatives
md: Contrastive training with in-batch negatives is what turns a language model into an embedding model: pull each true pair together, push everything else in the batch apart, with a scale (temperature) that controls how sharply.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Byte-level BPE: how GPT-2 and its successors tokenize anything
md: Byte-level BPE = UTF-8 bytes as the base alphabet (256 symbols, so nothing is ever unknown) + a regex pre-tokenizer that limits where merges can happen + an ordered merge list. Decoding concatenates bytes and is lossless.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
md: He et al. report that their 30-layer plain ReLU network trained with He initialization while the Xavier-initialized version *completely stalled*, with all gradients diminishing. Yet on their 22-layer model both converged (He init just started reducing error earlier), and on a smaller model the final accuracies were about the same. A bad init does not always crash; past some depth it silently stops learning.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Instrumenting a run: gradient norms, update ratios, activation stats
md: Log per step: loss, global gradient norm and learning rate. Log per layer: update-to-weight ratio (about 1e-3), activation std and dead fraction. Each failure in this course has a signature: shrinking scale with depth and ratios near 1e-8 for a bad init; ratios near 1e-2, dead units and a climbing gradient norm for too high a rate.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Dependencies and transitive trees: code you never chose
md: Misconception: "I only use five packages." You use five packages plus everything they pull in. Count with `npm ls --all | wc -l` or `pip list` inside a fresh virtual environment, and you will usually find one to two orders of magnitude more.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: SBOMs: an ingredients list you can query when the alarm rings
md: An SBOM is a claim about contents, only as complete as the tool that wrote it. It lists what is present, not whether any of it is malicious, and an SBOM made from source can miss what the build pulled in. Generate it from the built artifact, sign it, and keep it with the artifact.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
md: The question is not whether synthetic data enter the loop, but whether real data stay in it. Keep the original human data, keep adding fresh real data, and treat synthetic data as an addition. Even then, a fixed share of mismatched synthetic data floors the error, so its quality matters as much as its quantity.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When a system call blocks: sleeping, short counts and EINTR
md: Retrying `EINTR` is right for `read` and `write`. For calls with a timeout (`poll`, `epoll_wait`, `nanosleep`), retrying with the original timeout restarts the clock, so a steady stream of signals could stretch the wait without limit. Recompute the time left before retrying.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp
md: Trust strace's counts more than its times. Tracing stops the program at every call, so `-c` and `-T` times are inflated, and calls served by the vDSO never appear at all (the cost lesson). Measure speed without strace, for example with `perf stat`, and use strace to learn what the program does.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Taming the tail: hedged requests and honest reporting
md: Honest tail reporting: record every request into a mergeable histogram (HdrHistogram or bucketed histograms), measure from intended start under a load plan, merge histograms rather than percentiles across machines, and report several high percentiles plus the max, with the sample count.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
md: Test-time compute is not free at serving time. Every extra sample or thinking token is paid on every request, by every user. Training compute is paid once. That asymmetry decides when test-time scaling is worth it.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Thinking longer does not scale forever. s1's gains flattened after about six forced continuations, suppressing the stop too often led to repetitive loops, and the context window (the most tokens the model can read and write in one pass) caps how long one trace can be. Parallel methods (voting, PRM search over several traces) can extend scaling past that point; s1 found they complement sequential scaling.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Build a TTT-Linear layer: inner loop, dual form and outer gradient
md: Write the inner gradient as a formula and the whole TTT layer is ordinary autograd: the dual form is the primal form reordered into matmuls (equal to 1e-15), and backprop through time costs activation memory linear in $T$. On recall, $b = 1$ beat larger blocks in every run; how $b = 16$ compares with the whole sequence changed with the seed, so one run cannot rank them.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Thrashing at the boundary, and why two magazines bound it at 1/M
md: Two magazines per CPU, one loaded and one previous, guarantee that after every depot trip the CPU holds one full and one empty magazine. That alone bounds depot traffic at 1/M for any workload. Without the previous magazine, an alloc-alloc-free-free loop can send half of all calls to the depot.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Hunting in network data: rare, regular and unresolved
md: Every network hunt has benign twins. Software update agents and monitoring tools beacon perfectly regularly; some applications connect to fixed IP addresses by design; content delivery networks make 'rare destination' lists long. Attackers add **jitter** (random variation in the check-in interval) precisely to raise the CV. Combine signals (regular, rare, no DNS, unusual process) rather than trusting one.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Indicators: types, life cycle and decay
md: Every indicator needs a source, a first-seen and last-seen date, and a confidence. Load it, watch what it matches, and retire it on a schedule that fits its type: days for phishing domains, longer for behaviours.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: What a threat model is: four questions before the code
md: Threat modeling happens at design time and keeps happening. A threat model is maintained alongside the system and refined as it changes, not written once for an audit.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Design principles II: least privilege, two keys and shared parts
md: Principles pull against each other. Separation of privilege adds steps that strain psychological acceptability; least privilege adds roles that strain economy of mechanism. Saltzer and Schroeder call them warnings, not rules: when you violate one, write down why the trouble is accounted for.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
md: Symptoms of thrashing: `pgdemote_*` and `pgpromote_success` both climbing fast at the same time. Pages are moving down and back up. Either the hot set is larger than DRAM, or headroom is too small. Migration itself consumes memory bandwidth on both tiers.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: The TLS 1.3 handshake, message by message
md: Two messages carry the security: the **key shares** create a secret no eavesdropper can compute, and **CertificateVerify** ties that secret to the certificate's key. Without the signature, a man in the middle could run one DH exchange with each side.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
md: CUDA: *scalar program, blocked threads*. Triton: *blocked program, scalar threads*. In Triton you think about which tile each program owns; the compiler thinks about which thread holds which element.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Everything is a token: Chameleon and Emu3
md: Misconception: "sharing a vocabulary makes images and text equally easy to model." Image tokens have very different entropy (the average surprise of the next token, $-\sum p \log p$: high when many tokens are about equally likely) from text tokens, and the paper attributes the instability exactly to modalities of different entropy sharing one softmax.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
md: Unikernel speed comes from **removing the user/kernel crossing**, not from a faster CPU path. Gains are largest for small, syscall-heavy requests and near zero for compute-bound code.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: The spectrum: Linux-based unikernels, microVMs and sandboxes
md: These systems were measured in different papers, on different hardware, with different definitions of boot. OSv's 0.6 s, for example, used its ZFS filesystem; Lupine's authors found a read-only filesystem made OSv boot 10 times faster. Compare within one paper, or measure yourself.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Segments: immutable indexes, a write buffer, tombstones and merges
md: Tombstoned vectors are not free. They still occupy memory, and in a graph they are still traversed for routing. Heavy delete or update workloads need merges (and their CPU cost for rebuilding graphs) or latency and memory creep up.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and tuning verl in practice
md: verl in one sentence: a single Python controller expresses the RL algorithm as calls on WorkerGroups; each WorkerGroup runs a training or inference engine SPMD on a resource pool; batches move as DataProto or as TransferQueue keys; and actor and rollout share GPUs by sleeping and streaming weights instead of keeping two copies.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: The dynamics model: next-frame tokens with MaskGIT
md: Generating a frame is not one forward pass. Each frame costs a full MaskGIT loop (25 passes in Genie) over a context that grows with every frame. The paper's own limitations: Genie runs at around 1 FPS and is limited to 16 frames of memory.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
md: Decide by data and shift. Little data or a frozen-feature baseline needed: linear probe. Many tasks on one backbone or tight memory: LoRA (adapters are tiny and merge for free). Plenty of data from the deployment distribution: full fine-tune. Expect distribution shift at deployment: probe first, then fine-tune (LP-FT).

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
md: A common misreading is that the straight-through estimator makes quantization differentiable. It does not: it substitutes the identity gradient. The encoder is updated as if the decoder had received $z_e$, which is a useful but biased approximation that is better when $z_e$ stays close to its code.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass
md: A mixed batch is one flat list of tokens plus offsets. Backends with one variable-length kernel use it as is. Backends with separate decode and prefill kernels ask for decodes first, so one index splits the batch.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: What an image costs: provider token formulas and resizing rules
md: Resizing is silent by default. If your receipt is downscaled, small digits may become unreadable and any coordinates the model returns refer to the resized image. Anthropic's docs recommend resizing yourself first; OpenAI's guide notes images may be resized even with original detail.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
md: The template for almost every wait-free algorithm since: **announce** your operation in a per-thread slot, then **help** pending operations in an order that guarantees each announced operation gets its turn within a bounded number of steps.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
md: Every global score is an area-weighted average. Weights proportional to cos(latitude) count each unit of Earth's surface once.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authentication: enumeration, lockout, reset and skipped steps
md: Lockout and reset tests act on accounts. Run them only on accounts you created. A lockout test against a real user's account is a denial of service against that person.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Writing a report that gets triaged, fixed and paid
md: Write for three readers: the triager reproduces, the engineer fixes, the lead prioritises. Exact steps with your own accounts, evidence, plausible impact, reasoned severity, a suggested fix, and no one else's data.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Content Security Policy: telling the browser which scripts to trust
md: CSP is defence in depth, not a fix. A permissive policy with `'unsafe-inline'` stops almost nothing, and even a strict policy cannot help if your own trusted script takes attacker text and passes it to `eval()` or builds script elements from it. Encode output and validate input first; then add CSP.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Access tokens and the access check: how Windows says yes or no
md: Because the walk stops early, ACE order changes the result. Windows tools keep a canonical order: explicit denies, then explicit allows, then inherited denies, then inherited allows. Hand-built DACLs in the wrong order can grant access you meant to deny.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why a captured handshake allows offline password guessing
md: Changing the passphrase does not protect recordings already made: if an old passphrase is later guessed, every handshake recorded under it can be replayed into the PTK computation. With WPA2-Personal, the passphrase protects the past as well as the future.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app networking: cleartext, certificate checks and pinning
md: Leave certificate validation to the platform. The bug is almost always code that disables it: an empty trust manager, an always-true hostname verifier, a delegate that trusts any server, or a blanket ATS or cleartext exception. Pin only endpoints you control, and always ship a backup pin. Pins outlive app releases: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve keys after 2030, so plan rotation to post-quantum keys.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Why cosine forces you to fix the training length up front
md: Cosine couples the **shape** of the LR curve to the **end date** of training. You must choose the training length before you start, and every checkpoint before the end is half-annealed.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: sendfile: from the page cache straight to the socket
md: sendfile shares page cache pages with the network stack. The man page warns that the transferred part of the file must stay unmodified until the reader on the other end has consumed it. If another process rewrites the file mid-send, the bytes on the wire can be a mix of old and new.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
md: Two details. First, the bars show W p renormalized to sum to 1 for readability; the paper writes softmax(W p + b), which gives different numbers (T2 sports 0.911) but the same argmax, and the paper predicts with the argmax. Second, the bias is contextual: change the instruction, the examples, or their order, and p_cf must be measured again.
